findings.issue_text: pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go:30 — [P1, confidence 75] `return namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent` maps distinct authorization tuples such as `(name="a_b", parent="c")` and `(name="a", parent="b_c")` to the same denial entry, so a denial for one resource is returned for another resource.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go:154 — [P2, confidence 75] `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)` creates one backing-cache entry for every denied user/action/name/folder tuple with no cardinality bound, so a burst of high-cardinality denied checks exhausts the shared cache and evicts useful authorization state despite the 30-second TTL.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go:116 — [P2, confidence 75] `permDenialKey := userPermDenialCacheKey(...)` adds a second independently timed representation of the same permission decision, so a denial written immediately before `permCache` expires keeps rejecting a subsequently granted permission for another full TTL; the TTL only bounds the stale window, while deleting the denial cache field, key helper, lookup branch, and write branch removes the incoherent state and four maintenance sites.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go:973 — The test `"Should deny on explicit cache deny entry"` manually seeds `s.permDenialCache.Set(...)`, so the new `if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true) }` write path has no verification and a broken denial-population path ships while the caching suite remains green.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go:346 — The new anonymous branch `case types.TypeAnonymous:` reads cached permissions, but every added cache test uses `Subject: "user:test-uid"`, leaving anonymous Check and List cache behavior unverified and allowing anonymous requests to regress independently of the covered user path.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go:353 — The new identity dispatch treats `types.TypeRenderService` as an unconditional miss and shares the user cache branch with `types.TypeServiceAccount`, but the added tests cover only `types.TypeUser`, so service-account and render-service behavior can violate the intended cache policy without failing the suite.

pkg/services/authz/rbac.go:99 — The embedded-client path now constructs `authzlib.NewClient(... authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}), ...)`, but no test exercises this provider branch, so an incompatible no-op cache implementation or accidental embedded-client caching is not detected before release.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go:154 — [P1, confidence 100] `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)` starts a fresh denial TTL after evaluating an older permission-cache snapshot, so a permission grant made after that snapshot expires remains falsely denied until the later denial entry expires; although the denial TTL is bounded, it extends stale authorization beyond the source cache's own expiry and directly blocks the newly authorized user.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go:123 — [P2, confidence 100] `cachedPerms, err := s.getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` treats every identifier-lookup failure like a permission-cache miss and immediately reaches the second `GetUserIdentifiers` through `getIdentityPermissions` at line 139, so a degraded identity store receives two failing calls per Check request and doubles both backend pressure and request latency; although fallback is correct for `cache.ErrNotFound`, the code never distinguishes that sentinel from the upstream error returned at line 358.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go:982 — P1 confidence 100: The explicit-denial-cache test's `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}` contradicts its “Allow access” setup, so deleting the denial-cache lookup still produces `Allowed: false` through the ordinary permission/database path and the test falsely passes without exercising the behavior it claims to protect.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go:979 — P2 confidence 75 advisory: The sole denial-cache test injects `s.permDenialCache.Set(...)` directly and never drives the production write at `service.go:154`, so removing or mis-keying that write leaves the suite green and causes repeated denied requests to miss the new cache; although unit tests can isolate reads and writes, no separate test covers the write, so the rebuttal does not preserve change safety.

goldens.comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go:154 — [P2, confidence 75] `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)` creates one backing-cache entry for every denied user/action/name/folder tuple with no cardinality bound, so a burst of high-cardinality denied checks exhausts the shared cache and evicts useful authorization state despite the 30-second TTL.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that permDenialCache is created with shortCacheTTL (30 seconds based on context) and stores entries keyed by namespace+userUID+action+name+parent. The cache key function at line 30-32 shows high cardinality: `namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent`. For systems with many resources (dashboards), this could create many cache entries per user. However, this is an architectural/design concern rather than a bug - the code functions correctly. The finding raises a valid scalability concern about cache pressure, but it's speculative about actual impact. The 30-second TTL does provide some mitigation. This is a legitimate design consideration for the new caching strategy but not a verifiable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go:116 — [P2, confidence 75] `permDenialKey := userPermDenialCacheKey(...)` adds a second independently timed representation of the same permission decision, so a denial written immediately before `permCache` expires keeps rejecting a subsequently granted permission for another full TTL; the TTL only bounds the stale window, while deleting the denial cache field, key helper, lookup branch, and write branch removes the incoherent state and four maintenance sites.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a `permDenialCache` with `shortCacheTTL` that caches denial decisions independently from `permCache`. When a check fails, the denial is cached at line 153. However, if permissions are subsequently granted (e.g., `permCache` is updated with new permissions), the denial cache entry persists for its full TTL. The code at lines 116-120 checks the denial cache first and returns `Allowed: false` immediately without checking if permissions have been updated. This creates a race condition where a stale denial can override a valid permission grant, causing incorrect authorization denials for the duration of the denial cache TTL.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go:973 — The test `"Should deny on explicit cache deny entry"` manually seeds `s.permDenialCache.Set(...)`, so the new `if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true) }` write path has no verification and a broken denial-population path ships while the caching suite remains green.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' only tests reading from the permDenialCache (by manually seeding it), but does not test the write path where `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)` is called when `!allowed`. This is a valid concern about test coverage - the new denial caching logic at lines 150-152 in service.go has no test that verifies the cache is actually populated after a denial. However, this is not a bug - the code logic appears correct, it's just missing test coverage for the write path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go:346 — The new anonymous branch `case types.TypeAnonymous:` reads cached permissions, but every added cache test uses `Subject: "user:test-uid"`, leaving anonymous Check and List cache behavior unverified and allowing anonymous requests to regress independently of the covered user path.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the new `getCachedIdentityPermissions` function adds a `case types.TypeAnonymous:` branch (lines 346-351) that handles anonymous permission caching, but the test file only adds tests with `Subject: "user:test-uid"` which maps to user identity type, not anonymous. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly added nontrivial logic - the anonymous caching path in both Check and List operations is not exercised by any of the new cache tests (TestService_CacheCheck, TestService_CacheList).

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go:353 — The new identity dispatch treats `types.TypeRenderService` as an unconditional miss and shares the user cache branch with `types.TypeServiceAccount`, but the added tests cover only `types.TypeUser`, so service-account and render-service behavior can violate the intended cache policy without failing the suite.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that getCachedIdentityPermissions (lines 339-373) handles TypeRenderService by returning cache.ErrNotFound unconditionally, and handles TypeServiceAccount the same as TypeUser. The new tests in TestService_CacheCheck only test with 'user:test-uid' subjects, not service accounts or render services. This is a valid observation about missing test coverage for the new caching logic paths. However, this is not a bug - the code behavior is intentional (render service always misses cache, service accounts share user cache logic). It's an important non-bug issue about incomplete test coverage for newly added functionality.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/authz/rbac.go:99 — The embedded-client path now constructs `authzlib.NewClient(... authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}), ...)`, but no test exercises this provider branch, so an incompatible no-op cache implementation or accidental embedded-client caching is not detected before release.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that in ProvideAuthZClient (lines 101-105), the embedded-client path now uses authzlib.NewClient with a NoopCache. The NoopCache struct is newly added at the bottom of rbac.go. Looking at the test files in the diff, there are no tests that exercise the ProvideAuthZClient function or verify the NoopCache implementation works correctly with the authzlib client. The finding correctly identifies that this new code path lacks test coverage. This is a legitimate concern about missing tests for new functionality, not a bug per se.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go:154 — [P1, confidence 100] `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)` starts a fresh denial TTL after evaluating an older permission-cache snapshot, so a permission grant made after that snapshot expires remains falsely denied until the later denial entry expires; although the denial TTL is bounded, it extends stale authorization beyond the source cache's own expiry and directly blocks the newly authorized user.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real race condition in the caching logic. Looking at the diff, the Check function first checks permDenialCache (line 116-120), then checks cached permissions via getCachedIdentityPermissions (line 122), and if the cache misses or doesn't allow, it fetches fresh permissions from getIdentityPermissions (line 136). If the fresh check denies access, it sets the denial cache (lines 153-155). The bug is: if the permission cache was stale (outdated snapshot showing no permission), but the database has since been updated to grant permission, the code will still set a denial entry in permDenialCache. This denial entry will then block subsequent requests even though the user now has permission, because the denial cache is checked first before any permission evaluation. The denial TTL extends the stale authorization beyond when the permission cache would have been refreshed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go:123 — [P2, confidence 100] `cachedPerms, err := s.getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` treats every identifier-lookup failure like a permission-cache miss and immediately reaches the second `GetUserIdentifiers` through `getIdentityPermissions` at line 139, so a degraded identity store receives two failing calls per Check request and doubles both backend pressure and request latency; although fallback is correct for `cache.ErrNotFound`, the code never distinguishes that sentinel from the upstream error returned at line 358.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that getCachedIdentityPermissions at line 358 calls GetUserIdentifiers, and if that fails with an error other than cache.ErrNotFound, the error is returned. Then in Check() at lines 123-137, any error from getCachedIdentityPermissions (including identifier lookup failures) causes fallback to getIdentityPermissions at line 139, which calls getUserPermissions, which also calls GetUserIdentifiers again at line 377. This means a failing identity store gets called twice per Check request. The code doesn't distinguish between cache.ErrNotFound (legitimate cache miss) and actual upstream errors from GetUserIdentifiers, treating both as reasons to retry the full permission lookup.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go:979 — P2 confidence 75 advisory: The sole denial-cache test injects `s.permDenialCache.Set(...)` directly and never drives the production write at `service.go:154`, so removing or mis-keying that write leaves the suite green and causes repeated denied requests to miss the new cache; although unit tests can isolate reads and writes, no separate test covers the write, so the rebuttal does not preserve change safety.
